SEC9A-01.my_answer: the barn owl, its nocturnal counterpart,
SEC9A-01.convention: nonrestrictive appositive enclosed by matching marks
SEC9A-01.note: One rule really: paired punctuation. 'compound subject / plural hunt' is decorative - every option leaves hunt plural. Dash-open/comma-close distractor is a stock SAT trap. Same template as A-11.

SEC9A-02.convention: colon after independent clause introducing explanation; semicolon needs independent clause both sides
SEC9A-02.note: One rule (clause boundary). '; because' is the only distractor with bite; comma splice and fused options are standard. Not two interacting rules.

SEC9A-03.my_answer: October, the figures for the river wards,
SEC9A-03.convention: comma after long introductory dependent clause (CMOS 6.31) + nonrestrictive 'where' clause enclosed by matching commas
SEC9A-03.note: Genuinely two boundaries in one blank. The comma already printed before 'understate' settles the second boundary for anyone who reads four words past the blank; the first boundary (intro comma) is rule, not preference, at this clause length. Dash/comma mismatch distractor again.

SEC9A-04.convention: dash pair closure + verb agrees with subject outside the supplement
SEC9A-04.note: Two rules, both real, but the subject is literally 'two dissenters' so the agreement half is not hard. Clean 2x2 grid (mark x number).

SEC9A-05.my_answer: The supply ship having failed to arrive,
SEC9A-05.convention: nominative absolute set off by comma; finite-verb version would be a comma splice
SEC9A-05.note: Two rules (absolute vs finite clause; subject-without-verb in D). D 'The supply ship, having failed to arrive, the ... sledges were loaded' is a good trap. Absolutes are rare on the real test but the convention is unambiguous.

SEC9A-07.my_answer: the two that remain intact are illuminated
SEC9A-07.convention: restrictive relative clause takes no commas; no single comma between subject and verb
SEC9A-07.note: One rule (restrictive/no-comma); 'being' fragment is a second rule only nominally. Key is the only option with no punctuation, which a no-comma bias would pick - fine here because it is right.

SEC9A-08.second_defensible: ; Kofi Mensah, the customs inspector, (option A)
SEC9A-08.convention: semicolons throughout a series whose items contain commas (CMOS 6.60), including before the final 'and'
SEC9A-08.note: Two rules genuinely interact (series separator + appositive comma). Option A is the nearest thing in the batch to a preference call: some writers drop the semicolon before the final 'and'. CMOS and the SAT both require it, and A leaves 'the customs inspector, and Tomas Weil' ambiguous, so I keep exclusive=true, but this is the one to watch on a unanimity vote.

SEC9A-09.convention: dash pair closure + finite main verb; 'it' would double the subject
SEC9A-09.note: The 'comma before so' rule named in the explanation is decorative - all four options end with the comma. Effective rules: close the dash, keep a finite verb. 'it rarely colonizes' (resumptive pronoun) is the best distractor.

SEC9A-11.my_answer: the physicist Lise Meitner, his collaborator of thirty years,
SEC9A-11.convention: restrictive appositive (name) unpunctuated; nonrestrictive appositive enclosed by matching commas
SEC9A-11.note: Structural duplicate of A-01: coordinated pair, appositive on the second noun, closed by comma, plural verb follows. Same distractor set (semicolon/unclosed/dash-comma mismatch). One rule. Recommend keeping only one of A-01/A-11.

SEC9A-12.convention: dash (or colon) before a summarizing pronoun that gathers a fronted list (CMOS 6.86)
SEC9A-12.note: One rule but an unusual one; 'lime, that' is a real trap since the comma reads as a series comma. 'was' right after the blank tells the reader a main verb is coming, which helps eliminate the relative readings. Colon alternative not offered, so exclusive.

SEC9B-01.convention: neither/nor: verb agrees with nearer subject head (surveys); no lone comma between subject and verb
SEC9B-01.note: Two rules named but the comma half is weak - a comma between subject and verb is never tempting, so this is functionally a one-rule proximity item with one live distractor (identifies).

SEC9B-02.convention: not...but parallelism (to X / to Y) + fused-relative case set inside its own clause (object of judges)
SEC9B-02.note: Both rules genuinely load-bearing; strongest item in the batch. Caveat for the unanimity vote: whoever-as-object in fused relatives is tolerated by descriptivist references (MWDEU) and the digital SAT has largely stopped testing whom. Under edited-American prescriptive convention whomever is required, so exclusive stays true.

SEC9B-03.convention: ever since + past anchor requires present perfect; along with does not pluralize the subject
SEC9B-03.note: Two rules genuinely interact; have been is a strong distractor. Clean 2x2 (tense x number).

SEC9B-04.convention: opening participle must modify the subject; compound subject takes nominative
SEC9B-04.note: Two rules, but auditor and me concluded is transparently wrong to a module-2 student; reports and mine concluded is the only distractor that tempts. Demote from hard.

SEC9B-05.convention: agreement with head noun trusses across an interposed relative clause + not because / but because correlative parallelism
SEC9B-05.note: Two rules genuinely interact. but rather that / but that are non-parallel by rule, not preference (not that...but that would be the parallel alternative, and it is not what the first half set up).

SEC9B-06.convention: parenthetical opened with a comma must be closed before the verb + verb agrees with delegation, not members
SEC9B-06.note: Two rules, clean 2x2. The it inside every option gives away that delegation is singular, which flattens the agreement half.

SEC9B-07.convention: noun clause as subject takes singular verb + comma-opened parenthetical must be closed before the verb
SEC9B-07.note: Two rules genuinely interact; the plural nouns errors/passages sit right before the verb and the subject is a 10-word that-clause. Clean 2x2.

SEC9B-08.my_answer: but also the pattern books kept by its foreman offer
SEC9B-08.convention: not only must be answered by but (also) + verb agrees with the nearer subject head (books), not foreman
SEC9B-08.note: Two rules interact. Proximity agreement for not only/but also is the rule in CMOS/Garner; a notional-plural reading gives the same answer, so no second defensible. and also is transparently wrong, leaving one live distractor.

SEC9B-09.my_answer: the chief engineer, backed by two crews of local masons, was able to span the river
SEC9B-09.convention: opening participle must modify the subject + agreement across a comma-enclosed modifier
SEC9B-09.note: Two rules but engineer ... were is easy to spot once the dangling pair is removed. Demote from hard. Key is not the longest option (good).

SEC9B-10.convention: not only...but also joins matching elements; to is inside the first element so it must be repeated
SEC9B-10.note: One rule (parallelism). as well as is not a correlative partner by rule. Batch already labels this medium; agree.

SEC9B-11.convention: object of preposition in a compound takes objective case; comma-opened participial modifier must be closed before the verb
SEC9B-11.note: Two rules interact. myself as a compound prepositional object is attested (MWDEU) but every usage guide the SAT follows rejects it; exclusive stays true. Majority-vote tell: 3 of 4 options carry the closing comma and me appears twice, so picking the majority in each column yields the key.

SEC9B-12.convention: relative pronoun case set by role in its own clause; the board believed is parenthetical
SEC9B-12.note: One rule, done well - the believed trap is the classic who/whom hard item. which/whose are weak filler, so effectively a two-option item. Same caveat as B-02 about the digital SAT rarely testing whom.

drops_recommended: SEC9A-11 (structural duplicate of SEC9A-01; keep one)
holds_for_vote: SEC9A-08 (option A comma before final and - rule under CMOS 6.60 but nearest to a preference call)
SEC9B-02 / SEC9B-12 (whom items; prescriptively exclusive, but the digital SAT seldom tests whom)
two_rule_decorative_or_single: A-09 (comma before so is in every option)
summary.preference_vs_rule: No distractor is wrong only by preference. Nearest: A-08 option A (final-item semicolon), B-02 whoever, B-11 myself - all rule violations under CMOS/Garner and the SAT standard, tolerated only by descriptivist references.
cross_item_tells: Section A: 5 of 10 items (A-01, A-03, A-04, A-09, A-11) carry a dash/comma-mismatch distractor and it is never the key; in A-01/A-03/A-11 the key is the comma-both-sides option. This mirrors the real convention so it is a pattern, not a leak, but it is monotone.
A-01 and A-11 are the same template (coordinated noun pair + appositive on the second + plural verb) with the same distractor set.
Section B is a strict 2x2 grid (rule1 x rule2) on 9 of 12 items; the key is always the both-right cell. Standard SAT form, no letter/length tell. Key letters A5 B4 C7 D6.
B-11 is solvable by column majority (3/4 have the comma, me appears twice).
